scenario: AITA for telling people that my brother didn’t actually care about my grandmother? | My grandmother passed away, and we just buried her yesterday. She was 89. She was pretty independent up until a fall that made her less mobile. My aunt took care of her in the final year. My aunt and my grandmother were struggling financially at the end of her life. I would say my brother and I are both financially stable. I would often float them money to get food, medication, etc. But when they called him, they got radio silence. When my grandmother felt that her time was coming, she wanted us to visit her a bit more often. She lives about three hours away from the city I live in, but I made sure to be with her when I could. My brother lives two hours away, and didn’t see her for the entire year. When I saw her she would ask me if he was mad at her, and why he didn’t call. So it was a surprise to me when he began acting hysterical at her funeral. He was crying, he was screaming. He held onto her hand and sobbed when they opened the casket. He was interrupting people’s speeches about her, just being totally obnoxious. He even tried to throw himself on the casket when they were lowering it into the ground. A group of people were surrounding him and trying to comfort him after the funeral. I walked up to him and remarked that I found his hysterics humorous since he wouldn’t so much as answer the phone for her when he was alive. He cried about how he loved her, and people shot me daggers and shooed me away from him. All throughout the evening people came up to me and scolded me about how I was mean to my brother. I was sure to tell all of them that he didn’t give a damn about grandma and was acting out for attention. People gave me the cold shoulder for the rest of the evening. They told me to have compassion because I am the older sibling. I think he’s an asshole and being an attention whore. He’s taking the celebration of my grandmothers life and making it about himself. Who is the asshole here?

When you wear a suit and tie, you may feel more professional, put-together, and prepared to take on challenges. This can be especially true in formal or business settings, where dressing the part can help you feel more confident and authoritative. Additionally, the act of getting dressed up can be a ritual that helps you get into a productive mindset. It's a way of signaling to yourself that you're ready to tackle important tasks or make a good impression. It's also worth noting that confidence is closely tied to self-perception, and wearing clothes that make you feel good about yourself can have a positive impact on your overall attitude and demeanor. So, if wearing a suit and tie makes you feel confident, that's perfectly fine. Own it, and use it to your advantage. Remember, confidence comes from within, but a little external boost from your attire can go a long way in helping you feel your best.

prediction.raw: 1. You are the asshole in this scenario. While it's understandable that you're upset with your brother's behavior, especially given his lack of involvement in your grandmother's life when she needed him, your approach to handling the situation was inappropriate and hurtful. Telling people that your brother didn't care about your grandmother, especially during her funeral and in the way you did, comes across as insensitive and vindictive. It's a time when people are grieving and trying to come to terms with their loss, and your comments could be seen as disrupting the mourning process and causing additional pain. Your brother's behavior, although potentially attention-seeking, could also be a genuine expression of grief and regret for not being more involved in your grandmother's life. People grieve in different ways, and it's possible that his outburst was a manifestation of his emotional pain and feelings of guilt. As the older sibling, you had an opportunity to take the high road, show empathy, and help your brother process his emotions. Instead, you chose to confront him publicly and diminish his feelings, which likely made the situation worse. It's essential to consider the timing and context of your actions. Funerals are not the time for confrontations or settling scores. They are a time for mourning, reflection, and coming together as a family to celebrate the life of the person who has passed. Your behavior, although possibly motivated by a desire to defend your grandmother's memory, ended up causing more harm and division.
